name: Functional appliance orthodontics

card.summary: Braces-adjacent appliances (Herbst, Twin-block, Frankel) used in growing children to shift the lower jaw forward in Class II cases; trials show changes, with debate over how much is skeletal.
card.aka: Functional jaw orthopedics, Herbst, Twin-block, Frankel, Bionator, activator
card.note: Designed for growing patients with Class II bites; outcomes in adults or for facial appearance are not covered by the trials found.

quick.overview:
Functional appliances are orthodontic devices, fixed or removable, that hold the lower jaw forward in growing children with a Class II bite (overjet, a recessed lower jaw). The best-known are the Herbst, Twin-block and Frankel appliances.

The idea of guiding jaw growth appeals to looksmaxxing communities interested in jaw projection. Randomized trials in children found favorable changes in many treated patients, but these studies concern bite and jaw relationships in adolescents, not adult facial aesthetics.
quick.mechanism: The appliance repositions the lower jaw forward and the resulting muscle forces are intended to influence growth and the position of the teeth and jaw joint. A fixed Herbst uses a telescoping rod that lets the mouth open but holds the jaw forward when closed.
quick.risks: Reported drawbacks include initial discomfort and chewing difficulty, unwanted spacing, and failure to complete treatment with removable designs that depend on patient wear. Treatment is done by orthodontists.

lead: Functional appliance orthodontics is a group of treatments, using devices such as the Herbst, Twin-block, Frankel (FR-2), Bionator, Bass and activator appliances, that aim to modify jaw growth and bite relationships in growing patients, most often to correct a Class II malocclusion where the lower jaw sits behind the upper.[1][2]

The Herbst appliance is a fixed device with a telescoping rod that holds the lower jaw forward; Emil Herbst developed it in the early 1900s and Hans Pancherz reintroduced it in 1979.[1] A randomized trial of 215 patients aged 11 to 14 compared Herbst with Twin-block and found a lower failure-to-complete rate for the Herbst.[3]

Randomized trials of early (preadolescent) Class II treatment, including headgear or functional appliances, report favorable growth changes in about 75% of treated children in one study.[4] No studies found examine these appliances for aesthetic jaw change in adults.

paras: The Herbst is a fixed appliance attached by stainless steel frameworks to upper molars and lower premolars, with telescoping rods that let the mouth open but hold the lower jaw forward when closed. Variants include cast, acrylic splint and ball-joint designs.[1] The Twin-block, Frankel, Bionator and Bass are removable appliances.[3][5][6]

Orthodontists describe functional appliances as altering the position of the mandible so that muscle forces and joint adaptation change the growth relationship of the jaws and teeth. Studies have examined effects on the teeth, skeleton and the glenoid fossa of the temporomandibular joint.[7][8] The Herbst's effects on the masticatory system were studied with casts, cephalometric x-rays and muscle electromyography.[9]

A 2-phase randomized trial of early Class II treatment (overjet over 7 mm) found favorable growth changes in about 75% of children treated early with headgear or a functional appliance.[4] Related randomized reports examined early intervention and skeletal pattern.[10][11]

The UK multicenter randomized trial of Herbst versus Twin-block in 215 patients aged 11 to 14 found a lower failure-to-complete rate with the Herbst.[3] Other studies compared Twin-block and Frankel with untreated Class II samples, compared Herbst with Frankel, and compared Bass, Bionator and Twin-block hard-tissue effects.[5][6][12]
No studies found on effects on adult facial appearance.

According to Wikipedia, fixed Herbst appliances can cause upper-arch spacing and initial discomfort or chewing difficulty during the first weeks; severe underbites may require longer treatment.[1] Compliance-dependent removable appliances may not be completed by all patients.[3]
The appliances are discussed in appearance-focused circles as a way to guide jaw growth. The published trials concern bite and jaw relationships in children.

timeline.event: Emil Herbst develops the bite-jumping appliance.[1]
Hans Pancherz reintroduces the Herbst appliance.[1]
Pancherz publishes a survey of the Herbst's biologic effects and clinical use.[9]
Randomized trial of early intervention on skeletal pattern in Class II published.[10]
UK randomized trial compares Herbst and Twin-block.[3]
Outcomes of a 2-phase randomized trial of early Class II treatment published.[4]
